newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD sees better French growth, jobless tide turns.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees better French growth, jobless tide turns.

text.p: The French economy should grow by 2.5 percent this year and 2.8 percent in 1998 while unemployment -- now at a post-war record of 12.8 percent -- may have peaked, according to the OECD's June Economic Outlook report.

The report was prepared during an election which has swept a new left-wing government to power. Forecasts are largely based on the previous centre-right's economic policies but also assume continued state and social security spending restraint.

French economic growth, led by exports, started to pick up pace towards the end of last year to produce a 1.5 percent rise in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 but underlying inflation should stay close to one percent despite the outlook for stonger growth this year and next, the OECD said.
The public deficit in 1997 -- the year to meet criteria for European monetary union -- should hit 3.2 percent as a proportion of GDP.
This is above the 3.0 percent target but is the same as forecast for Germany and Italy, and the report predicts the deficit will shrink to the required 3.0 percent level in 1998.
The new Socialist-led government says the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting deficits to that level should be interpreted flexibly rather than in "dogmatic" fashion.

"The recovery has so far not been sufficiently vigorous to improve the labour market situation...(but) the rising number of job offers and temporary (work) agency employment over recent months suggests that the unemployment rate has probably peaked," the OECD report says.

France's unemployment level fell slightly in February, April and May but the jobless rate is still at 12.8 percent. The OECD expects the unemployment rate to fall to 12.6 at the end of 1997 and to 12.2 percent at the end of 1998.

"High unemployment has kept wage increases at a moderate pace and the underlying inflation rate has drifted down to below one percent due to low cost pressures and output well below potential," the report says.

"Export demand will probably be the main engine of growth. While private consumption should remain subdued in the near term, improving labour market conditions and a lower tax burden should bolster consumer spending later on and business investment should benefit from brighter demand prospects."
The OECD said its forecasts were based on expectations of continued export strength and better financial conditions.
"However, tensions in financial markets in the run-up to the introduction of the single (European) currency could dampen growth," it said.
On the other hand, the OECD added, "the saving ratio is at a relatively low level and a stronger rebound cannot be excluded".

OECD forecasters took into account the 1997 budget, plus the freeze of another 10 billion francs in spending credits and civil service wage rises announced earlier this year by the previous government, the report says. It also assumes "social spending growth somewhat above the official target".
The 1997 deficit forecast also takes account of the transfer to the government of funds from France Telecom covering future pension liabilities at the state telecoms operator.
The previous centre-right government had forecast economic growth of at least 2.3 percent this year and 2.8 percent in 1998.

New Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who entered office after a left-wing election victory on June 1, is expected to prepare a mini-budget with a focus on creating 700,000 jobs and boosting growth through increased consumer demand.
